metadata.title: Upper-Extremity Tendinopathy and Enthesopathy in the Athlete: Best Evidence in Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
metadata.abstract: Tendinopathy and enthesopathy represent common overuse conditions in athletic populations and frequently affect the upper extremity, particularly the rotator cuff, elbow extensor origin, and wrist extensors. These conditions arise predominantly from mechanical overload and are characterized clinically by load-dependent pain and impaired function. Following clinical evaluation, diagnostic evaluation frequently requires multimodality to exclude alternative pathology or inflammatory disease. Exercise-based rehabilitation remains the foundation of management, with contemporary evidence supporting progressive, individualized loading programs, including eccentric, concentric, isometric, and heavy slow resistance protocols, are tailored to symptom severity and sport-specific demands. Adjunctive modalities such as extracorporeal shock wave therapy demonstrate benefit in select chronic cases, particularly lateral epicondylitis and calcific shoulder tendinopathy. Although nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and corticosteroid injections may provide short-term symptom relief, corticosteroids are associated with inferior long-term outcomes and potential deleterious effects on tendon structure. Biologic therapies, including platelet-rich plasma and topical glyceryl trinitrate, demonstrate heterogeneous results, and high-volume image-guided injections remain selectively used in refractory cases. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms following 6 to 12 months of comprehensive nonoperative care because most individuals achieve symptom resolution without operative management. Open, arthroscopic, and percutaneous techniques demonstrate comparable outcomes. Emerging technologies, including in-office nanoarthroscopy and bioinductive collagen scaffolds, show early promise but require further high-quality investigation.

metadata.title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
metadata.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

metadata.title: Severe injuries in competitive cycling during an olympic cycle: injury patterns, time loss, and return-to-performance outcomes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cycling is an established Olympic sport associated with a distinct injury profile that has not yet been comprehensively investigated. This study aimed to retrospectively assess and analyze severe cycling-related injuries resulting in ≥ 3 weeks of time loss over a complete Olympic cycle. METHODS: A total of 192 cyclists were included, based on a retrospective online questionnaire assessing injury location, type, context, time loss, and return-to-sport outcomes. Comparisons by sex, discipline, and competitive level were performed at the athlete level using exact tests with 95% confidence intervals and were considered exploratory. RESULTS: Seventy-two of 192 athletes sustained at least one severe injury over the five-year period, corresponding to a proportion of 37.5% (95% CI 31.0-44.5). A total of 237 injuries were recorded, with the upper extremity (33.8%) and lower extremity (27.8%) being the most frequently affected regions. The most common diagnoses were hand fractures (n = 14), clavicle fractures (n = 13), and non-specific knee injuries (n = 9). Hand fractures (33.3%; p = 0.002) and shoulder dislocations (20.0%; p = 0.002) were most frequent among BMX athletes, while hand fractures also occurred more frequently in competitive athletes than in recreational athletes (13.5% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.001). Clavicle fractures occurred predominantly during competition and non-specific knee injuries during training. Mean time loss ranged from 6.5 weeks for hand fractures to 13.3 weeks for shoulder dislocations. Full return to pre-injury performance ranged from 85.7% after hand fractures to 28.6% after acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations. CONCLUSION: Injury patterns differed by discipline and setting, suggesting that prevention strategies should address both. The low rate of full return to performance after AC joint separations despite moderate time loss underlines the importance of distinguishing return to sport from return to performance in rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture. DESIGN: Systematic review. DATA SOURCES: Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively. RESULTS: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified. CONCLUSIONS: COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

metadata.title: Clinical Outcomes and Safety of Tendon-Derived Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy in Equine Tendon and Ligament Injuries.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Equine tendinopathies and desmopathies are common musculoskeletal disorders characterized by a limited regenerative capacity and a high risk of recurrence. Tendon-derived mesenchymal stem cells (TDSCs) represent a promising regenerative therapy due to their immunomodulatory and pro-regenerative properties. OBJECTIVES: This preliminary prospective clinical study aimed to evaluate the safety and potential efficacy of allogeneic post-mortem TDSCs, for the treatment of superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT) and suspensory ligament (SL) injuries in horses. METHODS: Nine horses were monitored longitudinally for up to 18 months following intralesional TDSC injection. Clinical outcome was assessed using subjective lameness evaluation, objective locomotion analysis with inertial sensors and standardized ultrasonographic examinations. RESULTS: The treatment was well tolerated, with no major adverse effects, supporting the low immunogenicity of allogeneic TDSCs. Overall clinical improvement was observed during the follow-up period and was consistent with improved locomotor symmetry measured objectively. Ultrasonographic findings suggested favorable tissue remodeling, including a reduction in hypoechoic lesions and progressive reorganization of the fibrillar architecture. However, treatment responses were heterogeneous, with SDFT lesions showing earlier clinical and ultrasonographic improvement than SL lesions. Nevertheless, this trend was not reflected in long-term outcomes, as only two horses, both presenting SL lesions, returned to their previous level of competition without reported recurrence. CONCLUSION: Allogeneic TDSCs appear to be a safe and promising therapeutic approach for equine tendon and ligament injuries. Nevertheless, their ability to reduce long-term recurrence remains uncertain and should be investigated in larger controlled clinical trials.

metadata.title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation. METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements. RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization. CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

metadata.title: Dose-dependent effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation combined with sprint interval training on performance adaptations in basketball players: a randomized placebo-controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sprint interval training (SIT) effectively improves physical performance in team-sport athletes, while sodium bicarbonate (Sb) supplementation may enhance training adaptations. However, the dose-dependent effects of Sb during SIT remain unclear in basketball players. Therefore, this study examined the effects of two Sb doses combined with SIT on physical performance adaptations in basketball players. METHODS: Forty trained male basketball players (age: 21.6 ± 2.0 years, height: 185.4 ± 3.5 cm, body mass: 84.1 ± 4.4 kg) were recruited and randomly assigned to four groups: SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb (n = 10), SIT + placebo (PL) (n = 10), and control (CON) (n = 10). The intervention lasted four weeks during the preparatory phase of the season. Participants in the training groups performed SIT three times per week in addition to their regular basketball training. The SIT protocol consisted of four sets of ten 5-second maximal sprints, with 20 seconds of active recovery between repetitions and 2 minutes of rest between sets. All 40 enrolled participants successfully completed the 4-week intervention, resulting in a 0% dropout rate. Performance assessments conducted before and after the intervention included countermovement vertical jump (CMVJ), standing long jump (SLJ), 20 m sprint, Illinois change-of-direction speed (CODS), Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 (Yo-Yo IR1), and Wingate anaerobic power (peak power output [PPO] and mean power output [MPO]). RESULTS: All training groups showed significant improvements in physical performance variables over time (p < 0.05). Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for all performance variables (p ≤ 0.001), indicating that the SIT groups showed more gains compared with the CON group. Both Sb supplementation groups demonstrated greater improvements than the SIT + PL group in CMVJ, SLJ, sprint performance, CODS, Yo-Yo IR1 distance, PPO, and MPO (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the SIT + 0.45 g·kg-1 Sb group exhibited significantly greater performance enhancements than the SIT + 0.3 g·kg-1 Sb group across all measured variables. CONCLUSION: Four weeks of SIT improved performance in trained basketball players, with Sb supplementation providing additional dose-dependent benefits (0.45 > 0.3 g⋅kg-1). While the higher dose yielded superior adaptations, its practical application should be balanced against potential gastrointestinal discomfort and individual tolerance to ensure long-term athlete compliance.

metadata.title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities. DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities. RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery. CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

metadata.title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes. METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class. RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk. CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

metadata.title: Breast Injuries in Women's Rugby Union: A Comparison of Prospective and Retrospective Surveillance.
metadata.abstract: Retrospective research has reported a high prevalence of breast injuries in women's rugby union (RU); however, most injuries are not reported to medical staff. This study compared the incidence and severity of breast injuries collected both prospectively and retrospectively over a comparable match exposure period. Prospective surveillance was conducted by clinicians (n = 14) using an online injury surveillance system across 140 RU players. Retrospective surveillance was conducted using an anonymous online survey completed by 370 RU players. Injury incidence was calculated per 1000 hours of match exposure. Severity was assessed using breast pain, bruising and swelling, ability to continue play, perceived effect on performance, and long-term breast changes. Three breast injuries were prospectively recorded over 1204 hours of competition (2.5 injuries/1000 hours). In contrast, 144 breast injuries were reported retrospectively over 5055 hours of competition (28.5 injuries/1000 hours). The retrospective injury rate was significantly higher than the prospective rate (IRR = 11.4, 95% CI: 3.15-41.73; p < 0.002). Ninety-six percent (n = 139) of retrospectively reported injuries had not been disclosed to medical staff. Injury severity was similar between surveillance methods, with bruising commonly reported, all players continuing to participate despite injury, and over half perceiving a negative effect on performance. Long-term breast changes were reported by 6% (n = 8) of players. The substantially lower incidence recorded prospectively suggests that breast injuries are underreported in women's RU. Improved reporting and surveillance strategies are required to better capture breast injuries and support female athlete health and performance.

metadata.title: Associations of cardiac autonomic modulation and urinary adrenal hormones with marathon finishing time in middle-aged male athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The autonomic nervous and endocrine systems are involved in the physiological adaptation to exercise, and in experimental settings both the sympathovagal balance and the adrenal function are associated with athletic performance. In this real-life field study, the association between non-invasive markers of cardiac autonomic modulation, urinary adrenal hormone levels, and marathon finishing time in middle-aged Caucasian male athletes was investigated. METHODS: A prospective study was conducted in male marathon runners aged ≥30 years. Continuous single-lead electrocardiographic (ECG) recordings were obtained using a wearable chest device from the day before the marathon until after its completion. Urinary adrenal hormone levels were measured before and after the race. Univariate linear regression analyses were performed to correlate general characteristics, nocturnal heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and hormonal parameters with marathon finishing time. A multivariable model was then applied including age, body mass index (BMI), and training hours. RESULTS: 104 athletes were enrolled in the study and 73 (median age 48 years, interquartile range = 16) had adequate data quality for the final analysis. Several HRV parameters correlated with better performance at univariate analysis; lower minimum nocturnal heart rate and vagal predominance, expressed as higher 2 Like Variations (2LV) values remained independently associated with shorter finishing time. Among hormonal variables, the post-/pre-race ratio of urinary normetanephrine hourly output and cortisol/cortisone ratio remained significant at multivariable analysis. Only BMI, but not age and training history, remained significant in a model integrating HRV and hormones. CONCLUSIONS: Under real-world marathon conditions, specific HRV indices and endocrine markers showed promising value as indicators of physiological readiness with endurance exercise in male master athletes.

metadata.title: Study of Transdermal Buprenorphine Patch versus Oral Etoricoxib for Postoperative Pain Management after Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Randomized Comparative Open-label Study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is a widely performed procedure for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, providing significant pain relief, improved joint function, and better quality of life. However, it is associated with substantial postoperative pain, which may delay mobilization, impair rehabilitation, prolong hospital stay, and increase the risk of chronic postoperative pain, thus making effective perioperative analgesia crucial for achieving optimal postoperative outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of transdermal buprenorphine patch versus oral etoricoxib for postoperative pain management in patients undergoing TKA, using Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) scores at rest and during movement for up to 1 week. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This randomized comparative study enrolled 88 patients of American Society of Anesthesiologists grade I/II after ethical approval. The patients were randomly allocated into two groups of 44 patients each. In Group A, patients received oral etoricoxib (90 mg), 1 h before surgery with a sip of water, and in Group B, patients received a transdermal buprenorphine patch (10 µg/h), 12 h before surgery. For statistical analysis, the Chi-square test and Student's t-test were used. RESULTS: Statistically significant differences were observed in VAS scores (at rest and during movement), with Group B demonstrating significantly lower pain. Furthermore, rescue analgesic requirements and length of hospital stay were reduced significantly in Group B, thus indicating overall superior postoperative pain control. CONCLUSION: Transdermal buprenorphine patch offers sustained analgesia (reduced VAS scores) with the potential for fewer systemic side effects, reduced need for additional opioid and rescue analgesic requirements, leading to shorter length of hospital stay.

metadata.title: Horizontal and Multidirectional Single-Leg Hop Tests Predict Isokinetic Quadriceps and Hamstring Strengths After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), isokinetic strength and single-leg hop tests (SLHT) are used to assess return to sport readiness. This study examined the relationships and predictive effects of isokinetic knee extension (Ex) and flexion (Flx) strength with 5 SLHTs at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR. HYPOTHESIS: There would be significant correlation between knee Ex and Flx strengths on the operated side and 5 different SLHTs; SLHTs would significantly predict knee isokinetic Ex and Flx strength. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3. METHODS: Fifty-one male participants underwent unilateral ACLR. Lysholm, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), and Tegner scales were assessed preoperatively and 6 to 8 months postoperatively. At the same follow-up, isokinetic strength at 60°/s, 180°/s, and 240°/s and 5 SLHTs were tested on both limbs. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, Pearson correlations, Fisher's exact test, and simple linear regression; limb symmetry index (LSI) cut-off was ≥85%. RESULTS: Isokinetic strength and single-leg hop (SH), crossover hop, and medial side triple-hop (TH) distances did not differ significantly between limbs (P > 0.05), whereas TH and 90° medial rotation hop distances were significantly shorter on the operated side (P < 0.05). Participants' Lysholm and IKDC scores improved significantly at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR (P < 0.001), but Tegner activity level did not change significantly (P > 0.05). High correlation was found between Ex strength at 60°/s and SH and TH distances on the operated side, and high-moderate correlations were found at 180°/s and 240°/s. Flx strengths showed a similar but slightly lower degree of correlation. Simple linear regression models revealed that especially SH and TH distances significantly predicted both Ex and Flx strengths (adjusted R2 0.26-0.52; P < 0.001). Among the LSI values, only a significant correlation was found between 60°/s Ex and TH LSI ratio (P = 0.01). CONCLUSION: The findings show that SH and TH tests were highly predictive of isokinetic knee strength after ACLR. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SLHTs after ACLR can be used as a practical and accessible complement to isokinetic measurements.

metadata.title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication. HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff. STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4. METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies. RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies. CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

metadata.title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks. DESIGN: Prospective study. SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported. PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes. RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042). CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

metadata.title: Discriminant and Prognostic Validity of the Multimodal Exertional Test (MET) for Athletes with Concussion.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exertional tests have become an informative tool to assist with clinical concussion management and return-to-sport medical decisions. However, current tests are resource intensive and thus, we developed a widely accessible, multimodal exertional test (MET). The objectives of this study were: (1) To evaluate the discriminant validity of the MET by examining sex-stratified differences in symptoms, heart rate (HR), and performance metrics between concussed and healthy athletes; and (2) To assess the predictive (prognostic) validity of the MET by determining whether week 1 MET performance predicts time to medical clearance. METHODS: This study was conducted at a single academic institution and affiliated sport medicine clinic in Toronto, Canada, with participants recruited between August 2022 and November 2024. 115 interuniversity athletes (female n=49, male n=66) completed the MET at off-season and 55 interuniversity athletes with concussion (female n=37, male n=18) completed the MET up to six times at 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-weeks post-injury. Average and maximum HR, symptoms, performance metrics, and MET pass/fail status were measured prior to and during the protocol. Probabilistic hierarchical models were implemented to estimate differences between concussion and healthy athletes (discriminant validity) and negative binomial analyses were used to examine whether MET performance predicted time to medical clearance (predictive validity). RESULTS: At 1-week post injury, concussed athletes exhibited greater symptom provocation during the MET compared to healthy athletes, with differences after each task. MET failure rates were highest during weeks 1 (63%) and 2 (49%) and declined through week 8. Athletes who passed the MET at week 1 recovered 20.6 days faster (90% Credible Interval [CrI] = 4.9-36.8 days, posterior probability [pprob] > 0 = 97.7%) than those who failed. CONCLUSION: The MET demonstrates discriminant validity by eliciting greater symptom provocation in athletes with concussion compared to healthy athletes. Improvements in symptoms and completion rates over 8 weeks indicate recovery-related gains in exertional tolerance. The MET also demonstrates predictive validity, as passing the test at week 1 was associated with faster time to medical clearance, supporting its potential utility as an early prognostic tool in concussion management.

metadata.title: Efficacy of Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Sampling in Muscle Tears and Intersex Differences in Professional Football Players: A Cohort Study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for monitoring the evolution of muscle injuries in athletes, although no established quantitative measure of recovery currently exists. HYPOTHESIS: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may provide a quantitative measure of muscle healing, and sex-related differences may exist in the evolution of muscle injuries. STUDY DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational cohort study. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a. METHODS: Twenty-six professional football (soccer) players (13 male ,13 female) undergoing MRI for muscle injury were retrospectively selected between October 2020 and June 2024. All athletes underwent MRI at baseline (T0) and at 2-week follow-up, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) acquisitions with b values of 0-100-800 s/mm². Two musculoskeletal radiologists measured ADC values within the index lesions at each examination. Changes in ADC between the two time points (ΔADC) were assessed using a paired-samples t test, while sex-related differences were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test. RESULTS: The overall mean ADC value at the lesion site decreased from 2.06 ± 0.35 mm2/s at T0 to 1.61 ± 0.30 mm2/s at follow-up corresponding to a mean ΔADC of 0.44 ± 0.20 and a 21.84% reduction. The difference between T0 and follow-up was statistically significant (t = 8.12; P < 0.001). Mean ΔADC values were 0.32 ± 0.20 mm²/s in male players and 0.56 ± 0.25 mm²/s in female players, respectively, with a statistically significant difference between sexes (z = -2.95; P = 0.003). When only hamstring injuries were considered, female players showed a significantly greater decrease in ADC over time than male players (Mann-Whitney U test; exact P = 0.02), with mean ΔADC values of 0.56 ± 0.30 and 0.26 ± 0.08 mm²/s, respectively. CONCLUSION: Muscle injury is associated with an acute increase in ADC values followed by a progressive decrease during healing. ADC may therefore represent a quantitative imaging biomarker for monitoring muscle recovery. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ADC measurement within muscle tears may provide a quantitative assessment of healing status and support individualized rehabilitation strategies in athletes. Sex-related differences may exist in injury pathophysiology and recovery patterns relevant to safe return to play.

metadata.title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
metadata.abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

metadata.title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
metadata.abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

metadata.title: Developmental Differences in Muscle, Tendon, and Cartilage Injuries in Elite Badminton.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated severe muscle, tendon, and cartilage injury characteristics by injury timing and post-injury management among elite badminton players. A retrospective interview study was conducted with 126 badminton players aged 19-24 years. A total of 87 severe injury cases reported by 73 athletes were analyzed, with some athletes contributing more than one case. Injuries were classified by timing into the secondary school group (SSG, n = 33) and the post-secondary group (PSG, n = 54). Injury characteristics and post-injury management were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, with effect sizes. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) examined associations with injury timing. Compared with the SSG, the PSG had higher odds of lower limb muscle injuries (OR = 6.00, 95% CI = 1.85-19.47, p = .003) and smash/stroke-related injuries (OR = 5.43, 95% CI = 1.15-25.66, p = .033), whereas the PSG had lower odds of lower limb tendinopathies (OR = 0.21, 95% CI = 0.08-0.55, p = .001). These findings suggest that severe injury characteristics may differ according to the timing of injury occurrence, despite no significant between-group differences in post-injury management, and may help inform potential injury prevention priorities based on the observed injury patterns.

metadata.title: The Impact of Tourniquet Duration on Postoperative Opioid Use and Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Tourniquet use during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains common, but its effects on postoperative pain, opioid use, and stiffness are unclear. We evaluated whether tourniquet duration was associated with pain- and stiffness-related outcomes after primary TKA. METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of 17,850 adults undergoing primary unilateral TKA at a single center from March 2016 to June 2023. Tourniquet use was categorized by inflation time relative to operative time as no tourniquet (n = 1,243), partial tourniquet (less than 0.6; n = 2,914), tourniquet-until-arthrotomy-closure (≥ 0.6 to less than 1; n = 10,003), or full-duration tourniquet (≥ 1; n = 3,690). The primary outcome was postoperative pain assessed by postoperative inpatient and cumulative 90-day morphine milligram equivalents (MME). The secondary outcomes were hours to clear physical therapy (PT), manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) within 120 days, and patient-reported Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) at six weeks. Multivariable regressions adjusted for covariates. The no-tourniquet group served as the reference. RESULTS: Partial-tourniquet use was associated with lower 90-day opioid consumption (-90 MME; 95% confidence interval (CI) -150 to -30; P = 0.003). Tourniquet-until-closure and full-duration tourniquet were associated with higher inpatient opioid consumption (+10 MMEs; 95% CI, 2 to 17; P = 0.015; and +14 MMEs; 95% CI, 6 to 22; P = 0.001), longer time to PT clearance (+2.7 hours, 95% CI, 1.0 to 4.5; P = 0.002; and +4.1 hours, 95% CI, 2.2 to 5.9; P < 0.001), and higher adjusted odds (OR) of MUA (OR 1.78, 95% CI, 1.14 to 2.79; P = 0.012; and OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.64; P = 0.040). Partial-tourniquet use was not associated with increased time to clear PT or increased odds of MUA. The KOOS JR scores did not differ significantly across strategies. CONCLUSIONS: Tourniquet use during TKA showed duration-dependent associations with postoperative outcomes. Partial-tourniquet use may represent a balanced strategy, associated with lower cumulative 90-day opioid consumption without the delayed PT clearance or increased MUA risk observed with longer-duration tourniquet strategies.

metadata.title: Association Between Early Postoperative Limb Symmetry Index Scores and 2-Year Patient-Reported Outcomes After Quadriceps Tendon Autograft ACL Reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The limb symmetry index (LSI) is a measure comparing strength and functional movement between the surgical and nonsurgical limbs, used after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) to guide rehabilitation and assess return-to-sport readiness. With increasing use of the quadriceps tendon autograft (QT-ACLR), limited data exist on whether the LSI score correlates with patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: To evaluate the predictive value of postoperative strength and functional LSI tests at 3, 6, and 9 months for short-term PROMs, determine Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) thresholds, and assess differences based on PASS achievement. It was hypothesized that quadriceps strength LSI score would more strongly predict 2-year PROMs than hamstring strength LSI score, and that higher 9-month isokinetic quadriceps LSI scores would be associated with higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Lysholm scores. STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. METHODS: Patients undergoing primary QT-ACLR from 2021 to 2024 with LSI testing during rehabilitation (isometric and isokinetic lower extremity strength, Y-Balance, hop testing) and no revision or additional knee surgery were included. The LSI score was assessed at 3, 6, and 9 months, and PROMs, including Lysholm and IKDC scores, were collected at a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years. Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate associations between LSI measures and PROMs after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to determine PASS thresholds. RESULTS: A total of 100 knees in 100 patients (mean age, 25.3 ± 11.2 years; BMI, 25.9 ± 6.5 kg/m2; 52% male) were included. Quadriceps and hamstring strength and functional performance progressively improved from 3 to 9 months, with the LSI score reaching 77% to 81% for quadriceps strength and 98% to 100% for hamstring strength by 9 months postoperatively. At a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years, the mean satisfaction score was 8.4 of 10, the Lysholm score was 90.7, and the IKDC score was 77.8. Linear regression, adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, demonstrated that 3-month isometric quadriceps LSI score had a strong effect on IKDC score, explaining substantial variance (β = 3.9; adjusted R2 [AdjR2] = 0.36; P < .03); 6-month isokinetic quadriceps and hamstrings showed moderate but significant effects (β = 2.9-3.7; AdjR2 = 0.13-0.17; P < .05) on IKDC score; and 9-month fast quadriceps had a strong effect explaining substantial variance in Lysholm and IKDC scores (β = 3.9-4.7; AdjR2 = 0.34-0.35; P ≤ .003). Lysholm and IKDC scores correlated with satisfaction and accurately discriminated PASS thresholds (area under the curve, 0.927-0.937; P < .001). Patients achieving the IKDC PASS demonstrated higher LSI scores across time points and all PROMs. CONCLUSION: After QT-ACLR, strength-associated LSIs were independently associated with PROMs at a mean 2-year follow-up, after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI. Early isometric quadriceps strength at 3 months predicted higher 2-year IKDC scores, with PASS achievers generally attaining a 60% to 70% LSI score by 3 months. Isokinetic quadriceps strength at 9 months predicted both IKDC and Lysholm scores. These findings highlight the importance of early quadriceps strength recovery and the value of LSI measures in predicting PROMs and informing early rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
metadata.abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

metadata.title: Low energy availability, disordered eating, exercise dependence, and injury prevalence in female CrossFit® athletes.
metadata.abstract: CrossFit® incorporates high-intensity, multimodal training with strong elements of community and competition. Despite known physical and psychological benefits, musculoskeletal injury prevalence ranges from 15 to 75%. Due to training demands, CrossFit® athletes may be at risk for low energy availability (LEA), disordered eating (DE), and exercise dependence (EXD), which may increase injury risk. Female CrossFit® participants (n = 198) completed an online survey including the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), Exercise Dependence Scale (EDS-21), and Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Participants were classified as DE only, primary EXD, secondary EXD (DE + EXD), or control (no DE or EXD risk). Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Overall, 37.8% of participants were at risk for LEA, 43.9% for DE, and 15.1% for EXD. Participants with secondary EXD had significantly (p < 0.001) higher EDE-Q global scores (3.9 ± 1.0) compared to primary EXD (1.4 ± 0.7) and control groups (1.0 ± 0.7). Additionally, 71.7% reported exercising despite injury, and 45.4% reported an injury within the past year. The prevalence of LEA, DE, and EXD was comparable to prior research; however, the high proportion of athletes continuing to train while injured suggests EXD-related behaviors may contribute to injury prevalence among CrossFit® athletes. These findings underscore the importance of early screening and education on adequate fueling and healthy training behaviors to support long-term health, performance, and injury prevention.

metadata.title: Large-Scale Evaluation of Performance and Biological Maturation in Post-PHV Youth Soccer Players: Sprinting, Jumping, Aerobic Fitness, and Functional Movement.
metadata.abstract: Akbaş, A, Hadyk, V, Bryk, P, Mazzei, S, Stanula, A, and Juras, G. Large-scale evaluation of performance and biological maturation in post-PHV youth soccer players: Sprinting, jumping, aerobic fitness, and functional movement. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to provide an integrated developmental profile of adolescent soccer players by examining how chronological age, biological maturation, and functional movement quality interact to shape sprint, jump, and aerobic fitness performance. A total of 246 male athletes (U15-U17) from 5 elite youth soccer academies completed sprint, jump, change-of-direction (COD), and aerobic tests alongside Functional Movement Screen (FMS) and Y-Balance Test (YBT) assessments. Maturity offset (years from peak height velocity, PHV) was used to estimate biological age, and group differences were analyzed using analysis of variance and analysis of covariance, with statistical significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements with age were observed in sprinting, jumping, and aerobic fitness (p < 0.001); however, after controlling for PHV, differences in jumping and COD performance were no longer significant, whereas sprint performance and aerobic fitness remained age-dependent. Functional movement and balance showed small age-related differences that were largely explained by maturational variation. Weak and inconsistent correlations between FMS, YBT, and performance (|r| ≈ 0.20-0.35) suggested partial independence between movement quality and motor output. Notably, in older players, higher scores in mobility-related FMS components were associated with slower sprinting, a pattern that may reflect-rather than cause-reduced mechanical efficiency associated with greater flexibility. These findings indicate that post-PHV players are not a homogeneous group and support the use of maturity-informed, multidimensional athlete monitoring to guide individualized training even after PHV.

metadata.title: Beyond Reconstruction: Return to Olympic Medal Performance Following Morphology-Informed and Criterion-Based Nonoperative Management of a Femoral-Sided Sherman Type II ACL Injury - A Case Report.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: ACL reconstruction and repair remains the predominant treatment pathway for elite athletes participating in pivoting sports. However, emerging evidence suggests that selected ACL injury phenotypes may possess healing potential, while objective criteria for identifying athletes who may successfully pursue nonoperative management remain poorly defined. Data describing elite athletes returning to the highest level of competition following nonoperative treatment are particularly scarce. The purpose of this case report is to describe the morphology-informed nonoperative management, criterion-based rehabilitation, and return to Olympic-level competition of an elite field hockey player following a fermoral-sided Sherman type II ACL injury. CASE DESCRIPTION: A 30-year-old male international elite field hockey player sustained a femoral-sided Sherman II ACL injury with preserved fiber continuity and synovial sheath during an Olympic qualification tournament. MRI demonstrated a meniscal ramp lesion and bone bruise. In the absence of subjective instability, a morphology-informed nonoperative treatment strategy was selected. Rehabilitation followed a criterion-based framework guided by objective assessments of strength, neuromuscular control, movement quality, and sport-specific function rather than time-based milestones. OUTCOMES: Comprehensive return-to-sport testing performed 86 days post injury demonstrated quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry indices of 99% and 98%, hop-test symmetry exceeding 90% and symmetrical gait mechanics. Running resumed at 73 days, unrestricted team training at 124 days, and international competition at 140 days post injury. The athlete subsequently competed in the Olympic Games final and achieved Olympic silver-medal performance 200 days after injury. Patient-reported outcomes returned to preinjury levels within 12 months. Follow-up MRI demonstrated preserved ACL continuity, ligament remodelling, and no evidence of rupture. DISCUSSION: This case challenges the prevailing assumption that ACL reconstruction and repair are invariably required for elite pivoting-sport athletes to regain international and Olympic-level performance. It highlights the potential importance of injury morphology, shared decision-making, and objective functional assessment when selecting treatment pathways after ACL injury. CONCLUSION: For carefully selected athletes with favorable ACL morphology, criterion-based rehabilitation combined with objective return-to-sport-assessment may represent a viable alternative pathway to reconstruction and repair. This case supports further investigation of morphology-informed and performance-oriented management strategies for ACL injuries in elite sport. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

metadata.title: Repeated sprint training in hypoxia as a post-surgical rehabilitation strategy: A case study in an elite badminton player.
metadata.abstract: Badminton is a racquet sport that imposes high demands on both aerobic and anaerobic capacity and involves repetitive, high-intensity movements, increasing the risk of non-contact injuries to joints and muscle-tendon units. Returning to sport-specific conditioning after injury, particularly post-surgery, presents challenges for deconditioned athletes seeking to restore aerobic capacity while minimising mechanical stress imposed on the injured parts. This case study evaluated the feasibility of integrating short-term repeated sprint training in hypoxia (RSH) as a supplementary modality within a late-stage post-lower back surgery rehabilitation program to support aerobic reconditioning before return to sport-specific conditioning. An elite men's singles badminton athlete completed 4-week RSH (FiO2 ~ 16.5%), alongside his regular rehabilitation schedule. The intervention consisted of 20 × 4-s all-out cycling sprints interspersed with 30-56-s recovery, performed once weekly. Post-intervention lactate profiling suggested a rightward shift in the blood lactate curve, with estimated increases of 33% and 10% in power output at the aerobic and anaerobic thresholds, respectively, indicative of aerobic reconditioning. However, the present findings should be interpreted cautiously due to observed stage-to-stage blood lactate variability, single-case design, and concurrent rehabilitation. Overall, the present study supports the feasibility of incorporating hypoxic RSH in late-stage rehabilitation to facilitate return to sport-specific conditioning.

metadata.title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
metadata.abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

metadata.title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
metadata.abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

metadata.title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
metadata.abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

metadata.title: Concussion Diagnosis, Management, and Functional Recovery: An Interdisciplinary and Evidence-Based Approach.
metadata.abstract: Sport-related concussion is a common and clinically complex form of mild traumatic brain injury with significant academic, occupational, and psychosocial consequences. Management has shifted away from prolonged strict rest to early, symptom-limited activity and targeted rehabilitation. Concussion remains a clinical diagnosis, and routine neuroimaging is typically normal. Symptoms may evolve over hours to days, and structured tools support early assessment; however, they should not be used in isolation to determine recovery or clearance. Office-based evaluation facilitates comprehensive assessment of symptom domains, comorbidities, and functional impact, and subsymptom threshold aerobic exercise testing provides a guide for early activity and individualized progression. Management includes therapies targeted to specific symptom patterns and interdisciplinary care for persistent symptoms. Pharmacologic therapy is symptom targeted and supportive, with limited evidence for select interventions and recommended avoidance of sedating agents that can confound monitoring. Nutritional and dietary supplements have theoretical benefit but insufficient clinical evidence for routine use. Functional recovery is addressed through individualized plans for return to learn, return to play, and return to drive. Prevention should focus on evidence-based risk reduction, with strongest support for policy and rule changes, and equipment and training interventions provide variable benefit. Emerging technologies are primarily research tools given limited standardization and uncertain clinical thresholds.

metadata.title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
metadata.abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

metadata.title: Editorial Commentary: Allograft Reconstruction in Chronic Proximal Hamstring Tendon Avulsions: Bridging the Gap May Not Equal a Full Return.
metadata.abstract: Proximal hamstring tendon avulsions are being treated surgically at rising rates, and although primary repair reliably restores function and return to sport in the acute setting, chronic and significantly retracted tears present a far more difficult problem. When direct repair is not feasible for a chronic, retracted proximal hamstring tendon avulsion, allograft reconstruction offers a bridge across a gap that would otherwise go unaddressed. However, significant chronicity and retraction are difficult challenges to overcome, and patient expectations must be appropriately counseled. As a salvage procedure, allograft reconstruction may improve patient outcomes significantly; however, it is not expected to restore full function, return athletic individuals to their baseline and preinjury level of sports participation, or match the success of primary repair. Allograft reconstruction may also carry more than double the risk of rerupture, which is important to discuss with patients up front. Graft choice and postoperative rehabilitation protocols remain heterogeneous across the limited available literature, and a validated tool to risk-stratify which chronic, retracted tears are best served by reconstruction versus continued nonoperative management does not yet exist. These findings suggest that allograft reconstruction is a viable and clinically meaningful option for a difficult, often nonoperatively unsalvageable problem, but surgeons should frame it for patients as a salvage procedure rather than a full restoration of function, and expectations should be set accordingly.

metadata.title: Adolescent Sports-Related Lower Extremity Pain and Overuse Injuries.
metadata.abstract: Adolescent participation in organized sports has increased substantially in recent decades, accompanied by a rising incidence of lower extremity pain and overuse injuries. Unique physiologic characteristics of the growing athlete, including open physes and periods of rapid skeletal maturation, combined with early sport specialization and increasing training demands, place adolescents at elevated risk for overuse conditions. This review examines common causes of sports-related lower extremity pain in adolescent athletes, including patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, bone stress injuries, and symptomatic flexible flatfoot. For each condition, we review epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management strategies. Most overuse injuries in this population are diagnosed clinically and respond well to conservative treatment that emphasizes activity modification, progressive rehabilitation, and load management. Imaging should be used judiciously, primarily to confirm diagnosis or exclude alternative pathology. Emerging therapies, including biologic injections and bone stimulation modalities, show promise in select conditions but require further high-quality evidence before routine adoption. Prevention remains central to reducing injury burden. Gradual progression of training load, neuromuscular conditioning, nutritional optimization, and monitoring during growth spurts are key strategies. Increasing evidence also suggests that psychosocial factors may influence injury risk. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinicians, coaches, and strength and conditioning professionals is essential to promote safe, sustainable sports participation and long-term musculoskeletal health in adolescent athletes.

metadata.title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
metadata.abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

metadata.title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus.
metadata.abstract: The extensor digitorum longus muscle and tendons are among the longer muscle-tendon units in the lower leg and foot. This feather-like, unipennate muscle is part of the anterior ankle group, attaching proximally along the lateral side of the lateral condyle of the tibia and the upper three-quarters of the fibula's inner surface. Near the ankle, the tendon narrows as it passes beneath the extensor retinacula and divides into four smaller tendons that connect to the toes. Since it crosses the ankle joint and attaches to the second through fifth toes, it facilitates dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toe joints. An accurate diagnosis of extensor digitorum longus tendonitis or rupture is crucial for appropriate treatment planning and optimal patient outcomes. Diagnostic musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSKUS) has become a widely used imaging modality for assessing many ankle and foot pathologies. It offers a portable, real-time, and cost-effective alternative that is gaining traction in rehabilitation and sports medicine settings. MSKUS has emerged as a valuable, non-invasive imaging modality for evaluating ankle and foot injuries. This manuscript reviews the utility of MSKUS in evaluating the quality, size, sonographic techniques, and clinical implications for rehabilitation professionals who need to visualize the extensor digitorum longus. By integrating MSKUS into clinical practice, providers can improve diagnostic accuracy, increase diagnostic confidence, monitor healing progression, and guide rehabilitation strategies to optimize outcomes for patients with ankle and foot injuries.

metadata.title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.
